introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2021. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections ». `regles_choix` porte une règle « 1 sur 3 » par section (A, B, C, D), ce qui correspond exactement à la consigne imprimée ; la consigne complète est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : chaque question porte 25 marks imprimés (« All questions carry equal marks »), soit 100 points pour les quatre questions à traiter. Aucun écart de points constaté ; `points` vaut 25 pour l'exercice et pour l'unique question de chaque fichier.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde et questions 1 à 12) ; publicités, filigranes gcerevision.com et mention manuscrite d'adresse web ignorés ; aucune question coupée ni illisible, aucune figure ni carte dans le sujet.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées au niveau Advanced Level (introduction, développement, conclusion argumentée). Aucune statistique ni citation n'est avancée ; les effectifs sont donnés en ordres de grandeur prudents (« roughly nine to ten million », « about two million »).

Question 2 : l'énoncé imprimé associe « the Jihad in Futa Jallon » aux dates 1854-1864. Ces dates correspondent à la guerre sainte d'Al-Hajj Umar Tall (empire toucouleur, parti de Dinguiraye, en bordure du Fouta-Djalon), alors que le jihad du Fouta-Djalon proprement dit date d'environ 1725 (Karamoko Alfa). Le sujet est recopié tel quel ; le corrigé signale la divergence et traite le mouvement de 1854-1864, avec le jihad du Fouta-Djalon en arrière-plan. L'année de début de la guerre sainte d'Umar est donnée de façon prudente (1852 ou 1854 selon les sources).

Question 2 : détails à vérifier par un historien (siège de Médine en 1857, prise de Ségou en 1861 et de Hamdallahi en 1862, mort d'Umar en 1864, chute de Ségou face à Archinard en 1890) ; ils sont cités conformément à l'historiographie courante, mais le corrigé ne s'appuie pas sur des chiffres.

Question 7 : les dates de 1688 sont données en style ancien (naissance du prince le 10 juin, invitation des « Immortal Seven » et acquittement des sept évêques le 30 juin, débarquement à Torbay le 5 novembre) ; le corrigé précise le choix du calendrier julien.
Question 4 : le massacre de Thiaroye (décembre 1944), les émeutes d'Accra (1948) et la conférence de Brazzaville (1944) sont cités sans bilan chiffré, le nombre exact de victimes étant discuté.

Question 5 : exemples de coups d'État (Togo 1963, Ghana 1966, Nigeria 1966, Ouganda 1971, Éthiopie 1974, Mali 2020) cités sans chiffres ; la formule « very many people were killed » remplace volontairement tout bilan sous Amin, très discuté.

Question 12 : la liste des suspensions et départs (Nigeria 1995, Fidji, Zimbabwe 2003, Gambie 2013 puis retour 2018) et l'adhésion du Cameroun en 1995 sont citées de mémoire historique ; aucun chiffre financier n'est avancé.

Questions à thème régional : les noms de thèmes sont qualifiés (par exemple `military coups in africa`, `refugee crisis in africa`, `league of nations`) pour éviter les collisions avec les Tags de l'Histoire francophone ; à reverifier à l'ingestion avec `find_tag_variant`.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Justify the view that the collapse of the Concert of Europe was inevitable after 1823.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The Concert of Europe (also called the Congress System) was the arrangement by which the great powers (Britain, Russia, Austria and Prussia, joined by France in 1818) agreed after the defeat of Napoleon in 1815 to maintain the peace settlement of Vienna and to settle problems by conferences. It was based on the Quadruple Alliance of November 1815 and met at Aix-la-Chapelle (1818), Troppau (1820), Laibach (1821) and Verona (1822). By 1823 the system of regular congresses had virtually ended. The view that its collapse after 1823 was inevitable can be justified by looking at the deep divisions between the powers. It must be added that the powers continued to meet in a looser form, so that "collapse" refers mainly to the Congress System as a mechanism for common action.

**1. Arguments supporting the view that collapse was inevitable.**
- *Different aims and ideologies.* Austria (Metternich), Russia (under Alexander I) and Prussia saw the Concert as a way to defend monarchy and legitimacy against revolution, and accepted intervention in other states' affairs (the Troppau Protocol of 1820). Britain regarded it only as a means of keeping the territorial settlement and the balance of power, and objected to interference in the internal affairs of states. Britain's 1820 State Paper (Castlereagh) stated this position, and Britain's refusal to support the Troppau principle was a turning point.
- *The test of the revolutions of 1820-1823.* Revolutions in Spain, Naples and Piedmont exposed the split. Austria intervened in Naples and Piedmont with the approval of the eastern powers at Troppau and Laibach, but Britain only protested. At Verona (1822), the powers agreed to let France intervene in Spain, and Britain, now under George Canning, refused to support it and withdrew from the congresses. French intervention in 1823 (the Duke of Angoulême's army and the capture of the Trocadero in Spain) restored Ferdinand VII, but it was done without British approval.
- *British interests and Canning's policy.* Canning preferred to act independently, protect British trade and avoid commitments in Europe. He opposed European intervention in Spain's American colonies; Britain recognised the independence of the Spanish American republics in the 1820s, and the United States announced the Monroe Doctrine in December 1823. This destroyed any chance of common action over the colonies.
- *The spread of nationalism and liberalism.* These forces were opposed to the principles of the Concert and the settlement of 1815, which ignored national feeling. The Greek revolt against Ottoman rule (from 1821), supported by public opinion across Europe, split the powers: Russia wanted to support fellow Orthodox Christians and expand in the Balkans, Austria feared revolution and Russian expansion, while Britain and France eventually joined Russia in the naval action at Navarino in 1827; Greece became independent in 1830. The Belgian revolt of 1830 and the French revolution of 1830 further showed the weakness of the system.
- *Rivalries among the great powers.* Russo-Austrian rivalry in the Balkans and Anglo-Russian suspicion over the Near East were fundamental and could not be solved by congresses. The death of Alexander I in 1825 and the changing governments in Britain and France removed the personal ties between the original leaders.
- *Weak machinery.* The Concert had no permanent institutions or enforcement, relied on unanimity and on the goodwill of governments, and so could not survive disagreements.

**2. Arguments against the view (limits).**
- The collapse was not total: the great powers continued to consult each other, and the London Conference of 1830-31 on Belgium showed that cooperation was still possible. Later meetings, such as the Congress of Paris in 1856 and the Congress of Berlin in 1878, kept the idea alive.
- Individual decisions mattered: for example, Canning's personal choices and Metternich's reluctance to accept change. A different British government might have continued the congresses.
- The preservation of general peace among the great powers until the Crimean War (1853-56) can be credited partly to the Concert.

**Conclusion.** The collapse of the Congress System after 1823 can be justified as almost inevitable, because of the basic conflict of aims between Britain and the eastern monarchies, the effects of nationalism and liberalism, and the lack of institutions. However, the Concert survived as a flexible practice of consultation, so what collapsed was the attempt to use it as a system of common intervention to suppress change.
